🇪🇺 European Union  Mixed  slow growth / ECB on hold
🇨🇳 China  Mixed  policy support / demand still soft
🇦🇺 Australia  Mixed  rate hike, households squeezed
🇵🇱 Poland  Bullish  banks and defence lead, metals wobble

body: Wednesday, February 04 2026 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto

Macro Stance: Activity is firm and the Fed is stuck in a political argument. The ISM manufacturing index for January came in at 52.6%, the strongest reading since 2022. Consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since 2014, and the January jobs report was pushed back by the partial government shutdown. A funding bill that ends that shutdown has now been signed. The Fed left rates unchanged in defiance of a president who wants them lower, and Kevin Warsh’s nomination as chair is being slowed by Senate Banking Democrats who want the Powell and Cook investigations resolved first. We stay Mixed: the activity data argue against a rate cut, the confidence data argue against overpaying for cyclicals, and the political path to a new chair is unresolved.

Rates & Curve: The 2-year Treasury yield closed the prior session at 3.57% and the 10-year at 4.28%, with the 3-month bill at 3.69% and the 30-year at 4.90% (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-03). The 10Y−2Y spread is 71 bps, and the 10Y−3M spread is 59 bps. Over 20 observations the 2-year rose 11 bps and the 10-year rose 11 bps, so the spread itself was unchanged at 0 bps; over five observations both legs rose 4 bps. The curve reads as “moderately steep, approaching the long-run average”, and the card’s move label reads “bear steepening (both up, 10Y up more)”. That label does not match the equal 11 bps moves on the two legs, so the call should rest on the level of the spread rather than on its direction of change. The S&P 500 closed at 6,917.81, down 0.84% in the prior session and up 0.23% over 20 sessions, while the VIX closed at 18.00 after rising 10.2% in the prior session and 20.8% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03).

New / Most Important: The most important story is the rotation inside equities rather than the rates move. Software and data stocks were hit by the AI-disruption trade: a new Anthropic tool sparked a rout that one headline puts at US$285 billion across software, financial services and asset management, and the threat of new AI tools was said to have wiped $300 billion off software and data stocks in a single session. Wall Street ended sharply down on those fears. The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.55% in the prior session and is down 0.25% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). On the policy side, the US–India trade deal cut tariffs on India to 18% in exchange for an end to Russian oil purchases, which lifts the mood for exporters but does nothing for the Fed’s problem.

Playbook ✓: Stay neutral on duration and trim software beta. Keep the 2-year as the anchor rather than adding 10-year length until the Warsh confirmation path is clear; a 10-year close above the 4.28% prior close with the 10Y−2Y spread widening would be the signal to trim duration. Hedge the S&P 500 through the software-heavy names that the AI-disruption headlines hit hardest rather than through broad index puts. Turn Bullish on US equities if the 10-year falls back toward its 4.17% level of 20 observations ago and the VIX gives back its 10% jump. Turn Bearish if the Senate delay turns into a longer blockage of the chair nomination and the 2-year moves above its 3.57% close.

Macro Stance: The euro area is growing slowly and the ECB is on hold. Output rose 0.3% in the fourth quarter, more than economists expected, but firms report deteriorating profits. Bets on a surprise ECB cut this year are a long shot, and a Bloomberg poll had the ECB locked on hold as calls for hikes faded. A Bloomberg note expects the ECB to leave rates unchanged at the next meeting. We stay Mixed: the activity data are not weak enough to force a cut, and the credit data are not strong enough to force a hike.

Credit & Inflation: The ECB’s survey of bank lending recorded an “unexpected” tightening, and euro-area banks are tightening access to business credit. Consumer inflation expectations are the outlier: euro-zone consumers lifted their five-year inflation forecast to a record high. Inflation is mixed on the price side: French inflation fell more than expected, while German inflation edged above 2%. The Bank of England is expected to hold at 3.75% with cuts still on the horizon. EUR/USD closed at 1.1799 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 0.71% over 20 sessions, and sterling was steady near $1.37 before the BoE decision.

New / Most Important: The sharpest European move is in the AI-disruption trade. RELX and Wolters Kluwer shares plunged on AI-competition fears, and the Guardian reported that Anthropic’s new AI legal tool had hit the shares of European data companies. Euro-area banks were the opposite: European stocks closed at records as banks led the rally. The digital euro is stuck in political deadlock in Brussels, which removes a policy catalyst for the payments and fintech names. Gulf exchanges stayed shut after Iran strikes, according to one headline, and European stocks dipped on the news.

Playbook ✓: Mixed: favour euro-area banks, which have the balance-sheet and rate-margin support, and avoid European information-services names that are exposed to AI substitution. The STOXX Europe 600 closed at 617.93 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 2.09% over 20 sessions, while the DAX fell 0.45% over the same period and the CAC 40 fell 0.70%. Turn Bullish on the broader market if the bank-lending survey stops tightening. Turn Bearish if the euro strengthens against the dollar while Bund yields rise further; the 30-year German yield has already reached its highest level since 2011.

Macro Stance: China is running two speeds: strong policy messaging and a strong onshore equity mood, against weak domestic demand and a property sector that has not turned. The official January manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3, the private survey shows factory activity expanding, and services activity picked up. The policy direction is supportive, but the credit and property data are not yet confirming it. We stay Mixed: the policy story is real, the demand story is not yet visible in the prints.

PMIs & Activity: The official January manufacturing PMI came in at 49.3, a contraction reading that one SCMP headline ties to weak domestic demand. A private survey reported factory activity expanding at the fastest pace since October, which is the conflicting factory reading the feed carries. Services activity picked up and hiring reached a six-month high in January, while the global manufacturing PMI showed cost growth at a three-year high. The official and private factory readings disagree on direction, so we weight the services and hiring data more heavily.

Credit Impulse: The feed carries no January credit print. The latest one is the December new-loan figure, which showed new lending shrinking to its least since 2018. The PBOC’s key bank loan rate fell to a record low, which supports borrowing costs but has not yet shown up in lending volumes in the feed. Beijing is trying to shore up the banking system directly: a $29 billion special-bond plan would recapitalise the biggest insurers. The confirming signal to watch is a January new-loan print that stops shrinking; until then the credit impulse is not a reason to add China cyclicals.

Property: Property has not turned. Sentiment on the market is “not fully back yet”, according to Hang Lung, and the sector started 2026 with a bleak sales outlook as sales declines accelerated. Developers say there are no real signs of recovery yet. Shanghai is buying small older flats to revive its ailing housing market, and China Vanke warned of an $11.8 billion loss for 2025. Hong Kong home sales slid in January. Property is the main reason to stay underweight the domestic cyclicals.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Policy messaging is pro-growth. A top official vowed to boost consumption to overhaul the economy, and Shanghai has set a target of 5% growth and global influence. The fiscal side is weaker: China undershot its 2025 spending goal in a sign of caution on debt and logged its first fiscal revenue drop since 2020. On currency, Xi called for the renminbi to attain global reserve-currency status, and the US has pressed China to let the yuan strengthen. Trade frictions are growing: the EU says it has received Chinese calculations for looming dairy tariffs.

Markets & Flows: The Shanghai Composite closed at 4,067.74 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 1.29% in the prior session and down 0.39% over 20 sessions. The Hang Seng closed at 26,834.77, up 0.47% over 20 sessions. The China A-share ETF ASHR closed at 33.24, down 1.25% over 20 sessions; the offshore internet ETF KWEB at 34.42, down 5.57%; the large-cap ETF FXI at 38.72, down 3.03%; and USD/CNY at 6.9463, down 0.6% over 20 sessions. Onshore retail is re-entering: 4.9 million new retail accounts were opened in January. Gold-linked flows are the opposite: China gold ETFs saw record outflows.

New / Most Important: The most important development is tax and policy headline risk in the tech complex, not the growth data. Chinese tech stocks were close to a bear market on tax concerns, after a rumour of a VAT hike knocked Tencent and other tech names. The Hong Kong market rose anyway, despite losses in tech, which tells us the index is being held up by non-tech names. Foreign houses are boosting their yuan forecasts: BofA has joined Goldman Sachs in lifting its yuan forecast, and the yuan is expected to rise this year, though Beijing has its reasons for saying not so fast.

Playbook ✓: Stay Mixed: favour onshore consumption and policy beneficiaries over offshore internet, and keep the yuan on a managed path rather than betting on a sharp move. The confirming signal is a January credit print that stops shrinking and a services series that holds its hiring gain; a second weak credit print would argue for holding offshore China exposure at a lower weight. ⚠ Divergence: onshore retail is re-entering the market at scale, with 4.9 million new accounts in January, while offshore tech is sliding toward a bear market on tax fears.

Macro Stance: Japan’s policy mix is in play before the lower-house vote. A poll had Prime Minister Takaichi’s party poised for a landslide, and a survey put the LDP–JIP coalition on track for a two-thirds majority. Inflation is cooling: core inflation slowed to 2.1%, the lowest since March 2022, while the BOJ debated the risk of being behind the curve. We stay Mixed: a strong mandate is good for the market’s fiscal story but worrying for the yen and the bond market.

Activity & Currency: USD/JPY closed at 155.4430 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 0.72% over five sessions and down 0.76% over 20 sessions. The yen is now a campaign issue: the Prime Minister’s remarks that a weaker yen brings benefits drew a finance-ministry defence, and tapping Japan’s forex reserves has become an election issue. Hedge funds revived their yen-weakness trades ahead of the vote, and the Japanese government bond sell-off is a live risk. The Nikkei 225 closed at 54,720.66, up 3.92% in the prior session and 5.57% over 20 sessions, after the record-high headline for Japanese stocks.

Playbook ✓: Stay Mixed: hold Japanese equities on a currency-hedged basis rather than adding unhedged yen exposure, because the yen-weakness trade is crowded and the policy response to a weak currency is political. Turn Bullish on the yen-unhedged equity leg if the vote delivers a clear mandate without a loose fiscal plan. Turn Bearish if the LDP’s landslide comes with a fiscal plan that worries bond investors and the yen keeps weakening past its 155.44 close.

Macro Stance: The RBA raised the cash rate by 25 bps to 3.85%, its first hike since late 2023, and left the door open to more. HSBC expects one more hike, and the central bank itself sees inflation staying higher for longer. We stay Mixed: the hiking cycle is good for bank margins and bad for the households that borrow from them.

Demand & Financing: Households are feeling the hike. Major Australian banks raised home-loan rates after the decision, and mortgage holders are being hit. Australian 10-year yields are heading toward 5%, and business groups are calling for a $50 billion spending cut to fight inflation. AUD/USD closed at 0.6956 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 3.61% over 20 sessions, while the S&P/ASX 200 closed at 8,857.10 AUD, up 1.47% over 20 sessions. Coinbase’s dispute with the big four banks over crypto debanking is a new access-to-finance issue.

Playbook ✓: Mixed: favour the banks while the hiking cycle lifts margins, and avoid housing-exposed property names where rate pass-through is hitting demand. Turn Bullish on the broader market if the next inflation print confirms the RBA’s view and the hike stays a single move. Turn Bearish if a re-accelerating print brings the second hike that HSBC expects into play, because household cash flow would then tighten further.

Monetary & Activity: The Monetary Policy Council held rates unchanged at its February decision, and one headline framed the cut as halted and asked whether the council will wait until March. The economy grew 3.6% in 2025, and the IMF has concluded its 2025 Article IV consultation with Poland. Industry is improving: the manufacturing PMI rose slightly, with the sector’s most optimistic reading in years. Poland’s growth is the strongest story in the region, and the rate pause is the main monetary risk to the bank trade.

FX & Markets: USD/PLN closed at 3.5768 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), up 1.03% over five sessions and down 0.49% over 20, while EUR/PLN closed at 4.2200. The iShares MSCI Poland ETF EPOL closed at 38.35 USD, up 6.03% over 20 sessions, and the WIG20 total-return tracker at 68.38 PLN, up 5.46%. Among the names, PKO Bank Polski closed at 96.50 PLN (up 10.34% over 20 sessions), PZU at 72.12 PLN (up 5.84%), PKN Orlen at 106.10 PLN (up 6.37%), and KGHM at 340.00 PLN (up 14.67%). Allegro closed at 29.14 PLN, down 7.1% over 20 sessions.

Companies: KGHM is the story with the most governance risk. Its CEO was dismissed and the supervisory board appointed a successor, and the stock fell 15% at the open on February 2 as the metals sell-off hit the Warsaw market. Allegro faces a lawsuit from the marketplace Erli, which accuses it of abusing a dominant position, and a court has ordered Allegro to show all delivery methods. Orlen and Poczta Polska dropped their plan to combine parcel-locker networks. Those three stories share a theme: state-linked or dominant companies under governance pressure.

Security & New Development: Defence spending is the structural bid. Poland signed a $4.3 billion “drone wall” contract to deter Russia, and Kongsberg-PGZ won a $1.65 billion counter-drone system contract. A defence ministry employee was detained on suspicion of working for Russian and Belarusian intelligence, which keeps the security premium in place. The domestic banks and the defence supply chain are the parts of the market that do not depend on copper prices.

Playbook ✓: Bullish on the domestic banks and defence-linked names, and use the WIG20 total-return tracker rather than single metals stocks until KGHM’s governance is settled. Turn Bearish on the broad index if the rate pause turns into a reversal of the cutting path. ⚠ Divergence: the WIG20 is at its highest level in 18 years, yet KGHM fell 15% at the open on February 2, so the index strength is coming from banks and defence rather than the metals leg.

Narrative: The consensus is that AI capex keeps semiconductors and hardware at the top of the market. The driver that matters now is the chip-supply tightness, which is pushing memory prices up and making the hardware trade a bet on pricing rather than volume. The technology sector ETF closed at 142.08, down 1.76% over 20 sessions and down 4.03% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), so the sector has already given back its earlier momentum. Memory prices are the key. TrendForce sees memory prices rising sharply into the first quarter, and Reuters reports chip prices surging 90–95% quarter on quarter. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are working to block memory hoarding.

Reported: Palantir beat Wall Street estimates on strong sales to US businesses, and its stock rallied. AMD’s forecast came up short of some expectations and the shares dropped; the company now predicts weaker first-quarter sales and its shares plunged on Nvidia comparisons. Nintendo shares sank 10% on memory-shortage worries even as profit rose. Intel’s chief executive said there is no relief on the memory shortage until 2028. Microsoft lost $357 billion of market value after a 10% drop on the Azure miss.

EPS Upside Watch: Micron is the most obvious memory-price beneficiary, with the shares up 34.37% over 20 sessions and up 2.24% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Business Insider calls the memory rally an AI supercycle with four stocks positioned to win. Intel is re-entering GPUs and has hired a chief architect, which is a longer-dated competitive threat to the Nvidia-AMD pair. Nvidia is nearing a deal to invest $20 billion in OpenAI’s funding round, but its own statements deny any rift. The set-up favours memory and equipment suppliers over the GPU vendors until the OpenAI relationship is clear.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says Nvidia is the safest AI stock, but OpenAI is reportedly unsatisfied with some Nvidia chips and looking for alternatives, and a CNBC analysis says the two giants appear stalled on their mega-deal. That cuts against the idea of Nvidia as the single winner of the capex boom. Apple concedes it is constrained by TSMC’s supply of advanced chips, which means the bottleneck sits in foundry capacity rather than in demand.

Narrative: The consensus is that the platforms are the AI monetisation winners. The driver that matters now is the earnings reaction to AI spend, with Meta and Alphabet the test cases. The communication services ETF closed at 117.74 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), flat over 20 sessions and up 0.72% over five. Meta soared after proving its AI spend, and it shares jumped 10% on a stronger-than-expected revenue forecast. Alphabet is near record levels, with traders ramping up long bets ahead of its results.

Reported: Meta beat Wall Street’s Q4 revenue estimates as AI spending rose. Disney beat expectations on theme parks and streaming, although its shares lost ground in the week after the quarter and the succession announcement. Alphabet has not yet reported.

EPS Upside Watch: Alphabet is the name set up for a surprise, with its results previewed for Wednesday and expectations for a record profit. Investopedia expects the stock to move sharply after the report. The risk is that the bar is already high: the stock has rallied 7.32% over 20 sessions into the print (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Meta has the momentum of a post-results rerating, but that is already in the price.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus treats AI spend as a reason to fear capex, yet the market rewarded Meta for spending and punished Microsoft for the same spend. The convention is breaking down: the market now pays for AI revenue, not AI spend, so a platform with cloud or ad growth can be rewarded while a peer with the same spend is punished.

Narrative: The consensus is that the banks are the cleanest way to own the rate and credit cycle. The driver that matters now is private credit: stocks of listed private-credit lenders plummeted on concern about exposure to the software sector, and the sector ETF closed at 53.53, down 4.63% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Blackstone and the alternative managers dived as software woes infected private credit.

Reported: Financials’ Q4 results put recession fears to rest, and Lloyds started a £1.75 billion buyback after an earnings beat. Santander beat earnings estimates and unveiled a buyback alongside its US deal, and it agreed to acquire Webster Financial in a roughly $12.3 billion cash-and-stock deal. Deutsche Bank posted its biggest annual profit in nearly two decades, but it is stuck with software loans in a rare hung deal.

EPS Upside Watch: The bank names with buybacks and deal flow are set up for upside, because capital return is the cleanest lever. JPMorgan’s stock picks favour financials over energy, and JPMorgan’s stock closed at 314.85, up 2.18% in the prior session. The risk is that the private-credit exposure caps the upside for the alternative managers and the banks that lend to them.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says a 2026 bank rally is simple, but a Chicago bank failure was the first US bank failure of 2026, and the software loans on bank balance sheets are the part of the book that AI disruption is hitting. The bank index is therefore not a single trade: the lenders with clean books should outperform the ones with software-heavy portfolios.

Narrative: The consensus is that oil is a geopolitical trade, and the driver that matters now is US–Iran diplomacy. The energy sector ETF closed at 51.67, up 10.19% over 20 sessions and up 4.03% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Brent closed at 67.33, up 9.02% over 20 sessions, and WTI at 63.21, up 8.38%. Oil fell as much as 5% on signs of US–Iran de-escalation, then edged up after the US shot down an Iranian drone.

Reported: Exxon beat Wall Street’s Q4 target as the Permian and Guyana fields took output to a 40-year high. Chevron beat fourth-quarter profit estimates and eyes Venezuela investment opportunities. Exxon and Chevron are declining new spending in Venezuela while they wait and see. Oil giants are bracing for a bruising earnings season with shareholder returns at risk.

EPS Upside Watch: Higher oil prices lift upstream names with the most unhedged barrels, but the Venezuelan supply story caps the upside. The US is set to issue a general licence for oil production in Venezuela, and Venezuelan oil exports rose sharply in January under US control. The set-up favours integrated majors over pure-play producers, because the integrateds have downstream and buyback cover if the supply story turns.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says a higher oil price is good for energy stocks, but the feed’s headlines tie the oil move to diplomacy and sanctions rather than to a tightening of physical supply. A broad de-escalation with Iran would cut the risk premium quickly, and the Venezuela licence adds supply, so the energy ETF is more exposed to a fall in oil than its 20-session gain suggests.

Narrative: The consensus is that industrials are a cyclical recovery trade, and the driver that matters now is the AI power buildout, which has turned gas turbines and grid equipment into the bottleneck. The industrials ETF closed at 168.94, up 5.69% over 20 sessions and 2.35% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). GE Vernova’s gas turbine orders surged 74% in the quarter, and Caterpillar has become a surprise AI play.

Reported: Caterpillar’s stock jumped after an earnings beat and demand for power-generation equipment, and the shares rose on the AI power theme. Lockheed Martin surged despite an earnings miss. Dow shares fell after a restructuring plan and steeper loss, including 4,500 job cuts. Siemens Energy is betting $1 billion that AI power demand will last.

EPS Upside Watch: The power-equipment makers are set up for upside because turbine backlogs are long. Caterpillar closed at 702.89, up 14.09% over 20 sessions and 10.01% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), so the easy move has happened. The next leg is more likely in names that have not rerated yet. Grid delays are a constraint on data-centre growth, and any easing of that constraint helps the equipment makers.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says industrials are cyclical and should lag in a slowdown, but the feed shows the strongest industrial moves are in AI-linked power equipment, which is structural rather than cyclical. The breaking convention is that the least cyclical industrial names are the ones rerating most, and a US state debate on making data centres pay full power costs is the risk to that rerating.

Narrative: The consensus is that consumer discretionary is tied to the labour market, and the driver that matters now is confidence. The discretionary ETF closed at 120.99, up 0.57% over 20 sessions but down 1.39% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since 2014, and consumer sentiment remains low. Starbucks’ CEO says consumer confidence is not matching the behaviour the chain sees.

Reported: Chipotle forecast weak annual sales and margin pressure as consumers cut discretionary spending. Starbucks missed on earnings but its traffic grew for the first time in two years, and its shares jumped. Walmart reached a $1 trillion market value as its e-commerce business boomed, which is a share gain but not a sector signal. Eddie Bauer is closing stores as mall retailers struggle.

EPS Upside Watch: The discretionary names with low-income exposure are set up for a surprise because the consumer is trading down rather than stopping. Walmart is the clearest example, with its value model and e-commerce growth lifting it to a trillion-dollar valuation. The risk is the tariff pass-through: companies could start raising prices due to Trump’s tariffs this year, which would hit margins for discretionary retailers without pricing power.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus is that a weak consumer means weak discretionary spending, but Starbucks’ traffic grew for the first time in two years and Walmart has just passed a $1 trillion market value. The convention is breaking as the value channel gains share, so the weak consumer is shifting spending to the cheapest providers rather than cutting it.

Narrative: The consensus is that staples are the defensive refuge, and the driver that matters now is pricing: consumers are pushing back on prices. The staples ETF closed at 85.87, up 11.01% over 20 sessions and 3.26% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). PepsiCo is cutting prices on Lay’s and Doritos as consumers push back, which is a volume-for-margin trade.

Reported: PepsiCo beat estimates as drinks sales picked up around the world, and its drinks sales are improving while it plans to cut snack prices. Walmart crossed $1 trillion in market value. Novo Nordisk warned on profits and sales amid the Trump drug-price crackdown, which is health care, but it shows how pricing policy is spilling into consumer names.

EPS Upside Watch: PepsiCo is set up for an upside surprise in drinks if the price cuts drive volume without eroding margins, but the snack-price cut is a margin risk. The set-up favours the drinks and value-retail names over packaged snacks, because the drinks business is recovering while snacks are being repriced.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says staples are the safest trade in a slowdown, but the sector is up 11% over 20 sessions while the consumer confidence data is at a multi-year low. The breaking convention is that defensives are now being bid for growth-adjacent reasons, which makes the sector vulnerable to a rotation back into cyclicals.

Narrative: The consensus is that health care is a defensive, earnings-stable sector, and the driver that matters now is drug pricing. The health care ETF closed at 154.10, down 0.61% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). The Trump administration’s most-favoured-nation drug pricing deals are under pressure, and Congress is about to overhaul the drug market.

Reported: Pfizer beat quarterly estimates despite a Covid-product decline and reaffirmed its modest outlook, yet its shares fell on the solid results. Merck topped quarterly estimates with modest 2026 guidance as generic competition looms. Zoetis cut its 2026 outlook as investors weigh slower visits and the pipeline. Amgen beat Street estimates and said patients need weight-loss options.

EPS Upside Watch: The names set up for an upside surprise are the ones with pipeline and pricing clarity. Lilly closed at 1,003.46, down 3.65% over 20 sessions, while the feed describes the obesity market as entering a new era with sales potential tightening. Novo Nordisk warned of a steep sales drop in 2026, which is the clearest read-across for the rest of the obesity group.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says a beat means the stock rises, but Pfizer beat and fell, and Eaton beat Wall Street’s estimates while its stock was down. The convention is breaking because guidance and the cost of the pipeline now matter more than the quarter, so beats are not rewarded in this sector.

Narrative: The consensus is that materials are a commodity-cycle trade, and the driver that matters now is the metals sell-off and the rebound. The materials ETF closed at 50.70, up 8.84% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Gold closed at 4,935.00 and silver at 83.04, both volatile after a historic plunge. Gold set for its biggest daily gain since 2008, and silver rebounded. Copper is an AI and grid-capex metal, and China plans to expand its strategic copper inventories.

Reported: Freeport-McMoRan’s stock is in the copper trade with a 20-session gain of 18.86% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Copper extended its slump on Feb 2 as traders eyed volatility across metals, while Citibank took profits on the Zambian kwacha after copper’s stumble. Australian investors piled into ASX-listed rare-earth names after the US stockpile plan.

EPS Upside Watch: Miners with copper and gold leverage are set up for a surprise if the stockpile policy holds. The US $12 billion critical-minerals stockpile is a demand signal for processors and miners that can supply to it, and Ivanhoe Mines’ shares rose on talks to supply the US Project Vault. Newmont closed at 117.14, up 13.15% over 20 sessions.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says gold and copper move together as risk gauges, but the feed ties gold’s crash to margin hikes and crowded bets rather than to growth. Copper is an asset here, not a gauge of China or global growth: its rebound is about stockpiling and capex, which is why it can rise while the broader industrial backdrop is soft.

Narrative: The consensus is that real estate is a rates trade, and the driver that matters now is mortgage pricing. The real estate ETF closed at 40.81, up 0.94% over 20 sessions and down 1.07% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Mortgage demand dropped 8.5% as rates rose to a three-week high, and rates are bubbling under 6%.

Reported: Rocket Companies jumped 6% after its CEO said mortgage loan volume is surging, which is a counter-signal for the lenders. Lennar shares jumped on a report that it is working on a Trump Homes plan, and US homebuilders are working on a plan to develop as many as 1 million homes. The housing market is swinging toward buyers.

EPS Upside Watch: The homebuilders are the set-up for an upside surprise if the government plan lands, but the mortgage rate is the constraint. Homebuilders are turning to the White House for help on an inventory glut, which is a sign that the sector is not yet selling through. Upside depends on the Trump Homes plan being real; the default is a further mortgage-rate drag.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus is that a housing market swinging to buyers is a bullish signal for real estate, but homeowners are falling behind on their mortgages and the sector’s largest buyers are using leverage. The breaking convention is that buyer-friendly headlines are coming from policy rather than from demand, so the rally should be treated with caution.

Narrative: The consensus is that utilities are the defensive yield trade, and the driver that matters now is AI power demand. The utilities ETF closed at 43.24, up 1.26% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). AI power demand is the reason the utilities are being re-rated, and the LNG market may swing from glut to gap by 2030 on AI power needs. Constellation fell 24.37% over 20 sessions even as the sector’s AI premium held, which tells us the market is selective.

Reported: American Electric Power is the safer AI trade, according to Barron’s. NextEra closed at 88.82, up 9.22% over 20 sessions. Power grid delays are challenging Amazon’s data-centre expansion in Europe, and Washington state is debating making data centres pay the full cost of power. Those are the constraints the utilities are being paid to solve.

EPS Upside Watch: Utilities with grid and generation backlogs are set up to beat, because the data-centre demand is contracted. The upside is in the regulated names with a clear capex plan, while the merchant power names carry the risk of a power-price cap. Vistra is down 6.09% over 20 sessions, which reflects that merchant risk.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says utilities are bond proxies that fall when yields rise, but the sector has held up while the 10-year yield is at 4.28%. The convention is breaking because the growth in power demand is overriding the rate sensitivity, and the market is paying for contracted capacity rather than for yield.

Narrative: The consensus is that European autos are a value and restructuring trade, and the driver that matters now is competition from China. The iShares STOXX Europe 600 Automobiles & Parts ETF closed at 45.60 EUR, up 1.39% over five sessions but down 4.39% over 20 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). One in ten cars sold in Europe is now made by a Chinese brand, and the Chinese EV makers’ shares skidded as sales slid after a tax incentive ended.

Reported: Germany’s auto industry faces a defining transformation, and Audi’s German workers renewed their opposition to a US plant. BMW closed at 87.64 EUR (down 5.8% over 20 sessions), Mercedes-Benz at 58.53 EUR (down 4.75%), and Volkswagen at 102.25 EUR (down 0.82%). Stellantis is set to face a Canadian claim of hundreds of millions owed to the government.

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up favours the names with the most US exposure and the least China-EV overlap, though upside is limited. Stellantis retailers started 2026 with momentum and a clear plan. The risk is that Chinese brands are coming to the US market sooner than expected, which removes the protection that US tariffs gave the legacy makers.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says European autos are cheap and undervalued, but the sector is falling even as the German economy grew. The convention is breaking because the cheapness is structural: software-defined cars are forcing European makers to rethink their independence, and that cost does not show up in the multiples.

Narrative: The consensus is that US–Asia semiconductors are the core AI supply chain, and the driver that matters now is memory and foundry capacity. The semiconductor ETF closed at 345.64, up 8.67% over 20 sessions but down 1.55% over five (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). TSMC’s US expansion is framed as insurance for Taiwan, and TSMC 2nm capacity is tight amid mobile and HPC demand. ASML closed at 1,395.88, up 13.65% over 20 sessions.

Reported: ASML’s Q4 call showed stable revenue and a slight EPS miss, and a headline asks whether it has signalled an exit from China. TSMC’s founder Morris Chang met Jensen Huang for dinner in Taipei. TSMC closed at 335.75, up 4.19% over 20 sessions. Chinese memory producers CXMT and YMTC plan to massively expand output amid the global crunch.

EPS Upside Watch: Foundry and equipment names are set up for upside because capacity is the bottleneck. Memory prices are rising further, and Western Digital added $4 billion to its buyback as AI boosted memory sales. The set-up favours TSMC and the memory-linked suppliers over the GPU designers, because TSMC is priced on capacity rather than on the OpenAI deal.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The consensus says Chinese memory is a threat to Korean and US suppliers, but the feed shows the global memory crunch is pushing even Chinese producers into expansion. The breaking convention is that the shortage is so deep that new supply from China is welcome in the near term, which makes the memory trade less of a China-risk trade than it looks.

Rewarded: The clearest reward in the last two weeks went to beats that came with AI revenue. Palantir beat fourth-quarter estimates on strength in AI and defence demand, and its shares jumped; the stock rose 11% after the report, with the market willing to pay for a 70% revenue jump. Meta soared after proving its AI spend, and its shares jumped 10% on the revenue forecast. Sandisk’s results drove the stock up more than 15% on better-than-expected quarterly figures. Caterpillar rose on earnings beats and demand for power-generation equipment.

Punished: Results with weak guidance or leadership questions were punished hard. Microsoft lost $357 billion of market value after its stock plunged, the biggest drop since 2020, because the Azure miss and the data-centre spend overshadowed the beat. PayPal shares sank on the CEO exit and a disappointing 2026 profit forecast, and fell 14.6% after the report. SAP shares had their biggest drop since 2020 after fourth-quarter cloud contract growth disappointed. AMD’s forecast came up short and the shares plunged.

Pattern: The pattern is that a beat is no longer enough. Pfizer beat estimates and its shares fell, and Eaton beat Wall Street’s earnings estimates while the stock was down. Merck topped estimates but gave modest 2026 guidance, and Zoetis cut its 2026 outlook. The market pays for AI revenue and for guidance that rises with it; it punishes capex without matching revenue and guidance that stalls. The beat is the price of admission, not the reward.

Attention into EPS: Into the next prints the market is focused on AI-linked revenue. Alphabet is previewed for Wednesday with record profit expected, but three red flags remain, and the stock is near a record with traders adding long bets. Super Micro reports after the close with Wall Street expecting 82% revenue growth. Reddit is being discussed as a stock to buy or sell before its Q4 release. Palantir’s post-earnings jump is being read by some as a risky pattern, which is a reminder that the rewarded names are the ones most exposed to a reversal.

Playbook: Own beats that come with raised AI-revenue guidance, and sell beats where capex or guidance disappoints. Into the Alphabet print, own the stock only with a defined risk, because a strong print is priced in and the market punishes guidance that merely holds. Treat the next Super Micro print as a test of whether the AI-hardware rerating can continue. Avoid pre-earnings positioning in software names where AI-disruption headlines are the driver.

Attention Gap: Most of the attention has gone to the chip rally, but the software and data sector has been losing value fast. An Anthropic tool sparked a rout that analysts put at US$285 billion across software, financial services and asset management, and the threat of new AI tools wiped $300 billion off software and data stocks. The problem has spread beyond the software names. Private-credit stocks plummeted on exposure to the disrupted sector, and Deutsche Bank is stuck with software loans in a rare hung deal. The attention is still on the mega-caps.

Exposure & Risk: The clean exposures are RELX and Wolters Kluwer in Europe, where shares plunged on AI-competition fears, and Blackstone and the alternative managers in the US, which dived as software woes infected private credit. The risk in those names is not the software companies themselves but the loans and fund values attached to them. Blue Owl and Ares have led private-market firms bashed by software risk. Use the listed managers as the hedge for the software theme, not as a bet on a recovery.

Trigger to Watch: The theme becomes consensus when a software company’s results show pricing or seat pressure from AI tools, or when a private-credit fund marks a software loan down. Watch the next software print and any lender disclosure of software exposure. Until then the trade is underowned because the mega-cap story has taken the attention.

Attention Gap: The market talks about AI chips and models, but the binding constraint is power. GE Vernova’s gas turbine orders surged 74% in the quarter, and gas-turbine crunch commentary is growing. Siemens Energy is betting $1 billion on AI power demand lasting. Attention on the power-equipment names is still behind the chip names.

Exposure & Risk: The instruments are GE, Caterpillar and utilities with generation backlogs. GE closed at 309.93, down 4.44% over 20 sessions, which means the rerating has not reached the turbine maker. Constellation fell 24.37% over 20 sessions and Vistra 6.09%, which points to merchant-power risk. The risk is that a regulatory move to make data centres pay the full cost of power delays demand for the equipment.

Trigger to Watch: The theme becomes consensus when the next order book from the turbine makers confirms the backlog, or when a major hyperscaler signs a long-dated power contract. A US state rule on data-centre power costs would be the first hard signal of a regulatory cap.

Attention Gap: Gold and silver dominated the headlines during the crash, but copper has been treated as a China growth gauge rather than as an AI and grid asset. China plans to expand its strategic copper inventories after the price rally, and China’s metals association called for an expanded copper stockpile. The stockpile story is being overlooked because the attention is on precious metals.

Exposure & Risk: Copper closed at 6.06 per pound, up 2.33% over 20 sessions and 4.5% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03), and Freeport-McMoRan rose 18.86% over the same 20 sessions. The risk is a supply-side or sanctions shock, which is why the EU is weighing a ban on Russian copper and platinum in new sanctions. Stockpiling is a demand signal that does not depend on China’s growth.

Trigger to Watch: The theme becomes consensus when the EU sanctions package is agreed with the copper ban in it, or when the US stockpile purchases start for the minerals it has announced. Watch the sanctions decision: a ban would tighten non-Russian supply and make copper a priced-in asset rather than an underowned one.

Attention Gap: Most emerging-market attention has gone to the Taiwan and Brazil rally stories, but Indonesia has had an $80 billion market rout. The regulator met MSCI after the rout, and MSCI has warned about the country’s market benchmark status. The attention is lower than the scale of the problem warrants.

Exposure & Risk: The exposure is to Indonesian equities through EM index and country funds, which the feed does not price. Nikkei warned that Indonesia’s opaque stock market risks a $60 billion outflow, and Reuters explained the government’s response to the rout. The risk is that an emerging-market status change forces passive selling, so position sizing should be small and currency-hedged.

Trigger to Watch: The theme becomes consensus when MSCI announces a decision on the market’s status, or when the Indonesian regulator shows a clear plan for market transparency. Until then the theme is underowned because the fear is priced but the outcome is not.

Market Context: Bitcoin closed at 75,633.55 USD on the prior completed daily close (2026-02-03), down 10.56% over five sessions and down 21.97% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance). Turn Bearish if bitcoin closes below its recent lows again on heavy volume.

Global Liquidity: Liquidity is tightening at the margin. Global bond sales reached $1 trillion at their fastest pace ever, and Oracle’s $25 billion bond sale is read both as easing fears of an AI debt wave and as a sign of anxieties about AI funding. Oracle plans to raise up to $50 billion in debt and equity this year. Warsh’s return revives tensions over the Fed’s $6.6 trillion QE hangover, and shrinking the Fed is proving harder than saying it. In Europe, the ECB’s bank-lending survey shows tightening, and in China new loans shrank to their least since 2018, with the PBOC cutting its key bank loan rate to a record low. One analyst attributes a $250 billion crash to a US liquidity crisis rather than to a broken crypto market.

Rates & Dollar: The US 2-year closed at 3.57% and the 10-year at 4.28%, with a 10Y−2Y spread of 71 bps; over 20 observations both legs rose 11 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2026-02-03). The dollar index closed at 97.44, up 1.27% over five sessions and down 0.84% over 20. Dollar disorder is a wake-up call for global investors, and the dollar risk premium is rebuilding. Long-end yields are the stress point: German 30-year yields are at their highest since 2011, and Japan’s government bonds are selling off. TLT closed at 86.76 (down 0.8% over 20 sessions), IEF at 95.53 (down 0.87%).

Credit Check: Credit is the weakest link in the equity story. Private-credit stocks plummeted on software exposure, and Blackstone and the alternative managers dived. A UBS worst-case scenario sees private-credit defaults hitting 13%, and the AI data-centre build-out is becoming all-consuming for debt markets. High-yield and investment-grade ETFs held steady: HYG closed at 80.72 (down 0.2% over 20 sessions) and LQD at 110.11 (down 0.33%). A State Street private-credit ETF hit a record inflow, which tells us the retail pipe is still open.

Equity & Fund Flows: Equity flows are rotating rather than leaving. Investors plowed billions into EM ETFs as diversification reigned, and global equity funds had inflows for a third straight week. China gold ETFs saw record outflows as metals slumped. Hedge funds trimmed North America exposure amid trade tensions, dollar pain and megacap weakness, and the yen-weakness trade is being revived ahead of the Japanese vote. Buybacks continue: Western Digital added $4 billion to its plan, and Lloyds started a £1.75 billion buyback after its beat.

Portfolio Implication: Liquidity is tight at the long end and rotating at the equity end, so the portfolio should lean toward quality duration and cash-generative equity rather than toward the credit-sensitive and metals trades. Keep duration near neutral while the 10-year sits at 4.28% and the spread is steady at 71 bps. Reduce software and private-credit beta, because the debt that finances the software names is the exposure that can reprice fastest. Keep the EM ETF exposure small until the Indonesian and Chinese flows clarify, and use the buyback names as the equity-liquidity anchor.

What Is Priced: The market is pricing a Fed chair who may be more aggressive on cuts than the rest of the committee. An economist said Warsh could shock markets with 100 bps of cuts this year, and Fed governor Miran still wants cuts this year. The confirmation is not assured: Senate Banking Democrats demanded a delay until the Powell and Cook investigations end, and Democratic senators sought to delay the nomination proceedings. Prediction markets also got the nomination wrong, according to Barron’s.

Conditional Expression: If the confirmation proceeds on schedule, buy the front end and the dollar on the view that a dovish chair is coming, and keep gold as a hedge against a politically pressured Fed. If the confirmation stalls, the 10-year is the instrument that reprices, because the term premium rises with the political risk. In that case, buy short-duration Treasuries against a 10-year position and keep the S&P 500 hedge through the software names.

Risk: The risk is that a chair who wants smaller Fed holdings tightens the balance sheet while cutting rates, which steepens the curve in a way the market is not pricing. The 2-year at 3.57% and the 10-year at 4.28% reflect a steady curve today; a sudden move in the 10-year would hit the duration trade first and the equity multiple second.

What Is Priced: Oil is pricing a diplomatic path with a military backstop. Iran’s president said Iran is ready to negotiate with the US, and US and Iranian nuclear talks are set for Friday, although Iran is demanding changes in the venue and scope of the talks. The talks are seen as a way to avoid conflict. Brent closed at 67.33 and WTI at 63.21, up 9.02% and 8.38% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03).

Conditional Expression: If the talks open on Friday, sell the oil rally: buy the broader market and sell energy against it, because the risk premium is the piece that comes out first. If the talks break down, buy XLE and the integrated majors, and buy the gold hedge. A military escalation is the one case where the energy premium overrides the diplomatic discount.

Risk: The risk is an incident at sea or in the air that turns the diplomatic track into a strike. The US shot down an Iranian drone and is worried about armed boats, and Trump has been using gunboat diplomacy after wavering on strikes. Those are the events that override the talks.

What Is Priced: The feed shows Ukraine talks as pending. Zelenskiy said new trilateral talks are set for February 4–5 in Abu Dhabi, and Russia struck Ukrainian energy targets with hundreds of drones and missiles just before them. Brussels is eyeing a new sanctions package as Russia pummels Ukraine, and the EU is weighing a ban on Russian copper and platinum.

Conditional Expression: If the talks produce a truce, the energy and defence trades respond in opposite directions: buy the European utilities and sell the defence-linked names that had the security premium. If the talks fail and the sanctions package is agreed, buy the defence and the Polish defence names, and sell the sanctioned-commodity exposure where it touches Russian supply.

Risk: The risk is that a sanctions package that bans Russian metals tightens supply in copper and palladium, which is the reverse of the risk-off move. The timing matters: a truce would arrive before the sanctions are agreed, which would remove the metals risk and leave the defence trade stranded.

What Is Priced: The market is pricing a strong mandate for Prime Minister Takaichi. A poll had her party poised for a landslide, and the LDP–JIP coalition is on track for a two-thirds majority. The yen is in play: the finance minister defended the PM’s comments on the benefits of a weak yen, and tapping forex reserves is an election issue. Hedge funds revived yen-weakness trades ahead of the vote, and the BOJ debated being behind the curve.

Conditional Expression: If the LDP wins a clear mandate without a loose fiscal plan, buy Japanese equities on a hedged basis and sell USD/JPY upside. If the mandate comes with a fiscal expansion that worries the bond market, the yen and the JGB curve move first: sell JGBs and sell the yen, and buy the Nikkei only on a currency-hedged basis. Japan is the one market where the vote affects rates, currency and equities at the same time.

Risk: The risk is a bond-market revolt. Takaichi has to face bond investors before winning over voters, and a Japanese bond sell-off shows the market is already testing the fiscal path. Japan has said no intervention was behind the yen’s run-up, and USD/JPY sits at 155.44, so the policy response is a live question.

Nvidia’s chief executive denies any rift and says there is no drama. The thesis is that Nvidia remains the AI capex anchor, but its own largest customer is looking for alternatives: OpenAI is unsatisfied with some Nvidia chips.

The dominant popular-narrative trade is silver, held through the SLV ETF and called the new meme stock, a pattern that resembles the GameStop squeeze of 2021 and the silver spike of 2011.

Why Retail Is Here: The crowd's story is simple: silver is a hedge against a debased currency, a metal that has rallied hard enough to become a favourite, and a liquid ETF makes it easy to own. The headlines have already picked up the name. CNBC asks whether silver is a meme trade and how the metal became 'GameStop in 2026', and Benzinga's headline calls silver the new meme stock. Retail investors drove silver to record volumes in late January, and a Binance headline asks whether silver is the meme stock of commodities and says gold and bitcoin find common ground. The attraction is that the story needs no earnings, only a price that keeps moving.

What Is Driving It: The price evidence sits in the card. SLV closed at 76.96, up 11.41% over 20 sessions but down 24.24% over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). The front-month silver future closed at 83.04 after a gain of 8.16% in the prior session, and it is up 9.03% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Gold moved in the same direction over 20 sessions, with GLD up 11.14% and closing at 454.29 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). The latest move is a rebound: CNBC reports that gold and silver rebounded and pulled mining stocks and precious-metal ETFs higher. The falls are the other half, because a CME margin hike stoked selling of gold and silver, and Bloomberg says gold is now behaving more like a meme stock.

The Social Signal: The attention is visible across the feed. Financial Post reports that silver's runaway rally has become a 'death trap' for Reddit's retail crowd, and on the writer's reading the forum is already arguing about the trade in public. CNBC reports that retail traders are not giving up on the SLV ETF even after silver's plunge, and on the writer's reading that persistence looks like conviction rather than panic. The institutional side comes through the same feed. Bloomberg reports that Citadel Securities' Rubner says the stock rally is at risk as retail fervor fades. The writer's reading is that a warning about fading retail fervor could also be read as a buy-the-dip signal. On that reading the debate has moved from 'is silver a meme trade' to whether the trade survives its own margin calls.

Historical Analog: The closest analog is the GameStop squeeze of January 2021, when a Reddit-led crowd drove a heavily shorted stock far above where institutions expected it to trade. CNBC's five-year look back asks how retail investors reshaped markets after that frenzy, and Robinhood's CEO has described a plan to avoid another GameStop buying halt. Institutional shorts were squeezed by a crowd that arrived on the story and the forum. The second analog is the silver spike of 2011. On the writer's reading, that run was driven by speculative buying and fears of currency debasement, and it reversed when exchange margin requirements rose and leveraged buyers were forced to sell. The 2026 parallel is in the shape, not the sequence: CNBC reports that a CME margin hike stoked selling of gold and silver, while retail traders are not giving up on SLV even after the plunge. The feed does not show which came first.

Smart Money View: The institutional view is split. The bull case comes from analysts. Forbes reports that analysts say the gold and silver crash could be short-lived, and a Yahoo Finance piece features one analyst who thinks $150 is just around the corner for silver. The price evidence fits that case for now: gold and silver rebounds lifted precious-metal ETFs and mining stocks. The other side is hedging and exit. Gold's record inflows from Asian ETFs were seen by some as a warning. Michael Burry warns that a bitcoin plunge could trigger a $1 billion gold and silver selloff, and Bloomberg reports that traders are weighing an unwind of 'crowded' bets. Reuters Breakingviews argues that options muddy gold's value as a gauge of global risk. The writer's reading is that the metal is less clean as a hedge than the crowd assumes, and that institutions are sizing the trade around the exit.

When the Narrative Breaks: The narrative breaks on levels the card can show. A close below the silver future's 20-session reference of 76.16 would erase its 20-session gain (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). The same test applies to SLV at 69.08 and to GLD at 408.76 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). The second trigger is margin: another CME hike would repeat the selling that followed the last one. The third is the crowd itself. If the Reddit crowd stops buying dips, even after Financial Post calls the rally a 'death trap' for it, the bid is exhausted, and a visible fade in retail fervor, the line Citadel Securities' Rubner uses, would confirm it.

Why Retail Is Here: The crowd's story is that the bitcoin-linked equities are a cheaper way to own the coin, and that a selloff in the stocks is a discount. Stocktwits reports that MSTR and BMNR dominated retail chatter after bitcoin's weekend selloff, while GME rallied, and another Stocktwits headline says the two stocks feel the heat even as bitcoin recovers. The attention is real even where the price is weak: MSTR closed at 133.26, down 19.1% over 20 sessions and down 4.56% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Retail reads the equity drop as a discount on the coin, which is the crowd's view rather than a valuation.

Bitcoin's prior completed daily close was 75,633.55, down 21.97% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Coinbase closed at 179.66, down 29.52% over 20 sessions, and IBIT at 43.30, down 19.0% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2026-02-03). Michael Burry warns that a bitcoin plunge could trigger a $1 billion gold and silver selloff, a reminder that the stress spreads beyond crypto.
